Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0% . Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window . The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings. items.title: Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux
items.summary:
The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load.

Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs.

To help maintainers handle the load and catch bugs before they land, the Google AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko, an open-source, agentic code review system powered by Gemini. We named the project after the Japanese word 刺し子, a stitching technique for artistically reinforcing worn cloth, and donated it to the Linux Foundation earlier this year.

In this blog, we cover the problem Sashiko was designed to solve, how it works, what the data shows, and what we learned from building and running it in the wild.

Reviewing code is hard

Reviewing a change in a complex code base is objectively hard, both for humans and LLMs. It often requires a deep understanding of how the system works in general, well outside the proposed change. In fact, it’s pretty common to see patches that engineers claim perfectly solve the problem, but if they were to be merged, would actually introduce even worse problems (albeit subtle). Traditionally, only experienced maintainers have been able to spot and prevent these issues. The same is true for agentically generated code.

To verify the correctness of a change, a potentially large number of invariants should be proven, which is often a much larger and harder task than developing the change itself. This is true for both human and agentic reviewers. However, LLM-based reviewers have some unique properties, both positive and negative:

  1. LLMs often struggle to put in enough effort. LLMs are trained to achieve the goal of spending fewer tokens. So they often tend to cut corners and dismiss concerns without proper investigation or flag false positives without proper due diligence.
  2. LLMs are easier to bias. The current generation of LLMs usually performs much better if provided a single relatively simple task (e.g., prove the patch for memory leaks) rather than multiple tasks (e.g., explore several complex, varied concerns). It’s pretty common for an LLM to find an obvious issue in the code and refuse to look deeper for other types of issues. Also, commit log text can sometimes affect the result of code review in a non-predicatable or even malicious way.
  3. LLMs don’t have persistent memory. Surprisingly, this is a positive thing for code review: An LLM can review the same or similar patch multiple times as if it were a new patch. No sane human can review the same patch applied to 100 slightly different branches to find the few that have incompatible changes.

How Sashiko reviews a patch

To avoid these failure modes, Sashiko separates finding candidate bugs from verification of those bugs, and requires each pass to record what it ruled out:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Gather context and plan\r\n -> Parallel specialist sessions (concerns + dismissed concerns)\r\n -> Triage\r\n -> Per-bug deep checks\r\n -> Review report'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f19fbb2b550>)])]>

Notes on each step:

  1. Gather context and plan: Sashiko first pulls in the code around the diff (modified functions, struct definitions, and direct callers) and loads the subsystem's domain guides, so the changed lines are never judged in isolation. A planner then decides which specialist passes are needed (skipping hardware checks on pure software code, for example) and sets a reasoning budget for each pass based on patch complexity.

  2. Parallel specialist sessions: Up to seven specialist sessions run in parallel, each focused on a single class of problems: commit intent, implementation match, control flow, resource lifetimes, locking, security, and hardware. Giving each pass a single focus prevents one type of bug from crowding out another. Each session searches and reads the repository with git tools (averaging about 100 tool calls per review) and outputs two lists: concerns it believes are real, and candidate concerns it investigated and ruled out, along with the code that supports that conclusion.

  3. Triage: A lead verifier audits those two lists together. Clear-cut bugs already proven by the code in front of it pass straight through; dismissals proven by a local check are dropped. Everything else deserves additional investigation. Crucially, that includes not only contested bugs where specialists disagreed, but also shaky self-dismissals — cases where a specialist spotted a real bug and dismissed it by assuming, without proof, that some unseen caller or lock would prevent it.

  4. Per-bug deep checks: Instead of checking all difficult cases in one shared prompt, Sashiko gives each difficult case its own verification agent that runs in parallel. Each agent gets one specific question to answer with git tools under a symmetrical rule: Neither a bug claim nor a dismissal is accepted without concrete code proof across all call sites. If a specialist talks itself out of a real bug based on a false assumption, this step catches it and promotes it back to a real finding.

  5. Review report: Sashiko generates a report that sounds like a human maintainer asking questions about the proposed change, matching the style expected on a Linux mailing list.

All this happens at no cost for developers. Deep agentic reviews at scale require a substantial token budget. If developers had to pay for them with their own API keys, many important contributors would be pushed away. Instead, Sashiko reviews patches sent to public Linux kernel mailing lists, and Google runs the service at sashiko.dev. Everything runs in the open: every prompt, tool call, reasoning step, and ruled-out bug is public. The project initially used the open-source Linux review prompts started by Chris Mason, and more than 100 contributors, including prominent kernel maintainers and engineers, have since helped to improve prompts and Sashiko itself. Recently, Sashiko switched to a different prompt system that combines per-tree or per-version auto-generated notes on code with subjective maintainers notes, which contain directions and instructions from maintainers that can’t be derived from the code.

What the data shows

The real test of an automated reviewer is whether maintainers pay attention to the reports it sends out, and whether those reports track actual software quality. Seven months of Sashiko production data from the kernel mailing lists give a clear picture of both these questions.

It is part of the daily workflow. Sashiko completes roughly 1200 reviews a day across over 100 kernel mailing lists. It sends review emails only to lists whose maintainers opt in, and already over 70 of them have done so. Developers also engage directly with the reports: More than 1500 kernel developers have replied on the mailing lists, and their pushback on false alarms has directly driven improvements to Sashiko's prompts and verification engine. In fact, LWN.net recently wrote that Sashiko has already become an important part of the kernel's development process and was the top bug reporter of issues in the 7.2 release cycle.

It prevents new bugs and uncovers old ones. When Sashiko flags a bug in a proposed patch, the author typically fixes it in the next revision before the change is ever merged. Many developers run Sashiko locally or in corporate private instances. The bugs that Sashiko helped to prevent leave no trace in the git commit log, making them hard to count directly. What can be counted are fixes for preexisting bugs that Sashiko finds and reports as a byproduct of reviewing new changes: Sashiko is cited in over 2000 mainline kernel commits and in over 500 of this year's official Linux kernel CVEs, spanning drivers, core kernel code, networking, GPUs, memory management, and virtualization.

Fewer bugs are slipping into mainline releases. Across the 18 kernel releases prior to Sashiko (Linux 6.2 through 6.19, covering 254000 commits), an average of 3.4% of merged commits required a follow-up fix within 60 days. Since Sashiko rolled out, that 60-day fix rate has fallen to 2.8% in Linux 7.1 and 2.2% in Linux 7.2, a 35% drop (with the 30-day fix rate falling from 2.3% to 1.4%). It’s too early to make strong claims, and obviously many other factors can influence release-to-release numbers, so we cannot solely credit Sashiko for the entire drop, but the trend is optimistic.

Since Sashiko was rolled out, the percentage of merged commits in the Linux kernel that received a follow-up fix in 60 days has dropped by 35%.

A clean review carries real signal. If Sashiko's warnings were mostly noise, commits merged with warnings would need follow-up fixes no more often than commits that passed cleanly. In practice, across 21,500 tracked mainline commits, patches that received a clean Sashiko review required a follow-up fix within 60 days just 0.9% of the time — less than a third of the historical baseline. Patches merged despite a critical Sashiko warning needed a fix 7.6% of the time — an 8x higher risk (and 6.3x higher even after adjusting for patch size). 

That gap is what makes Sashiko useful to maintainers: A clean pass instills real confidence, while a critical warning is a strong reason to take another look at the proposed patch.

This all tracks with what Linus Torvalds wrote in a mailing-list discussion a few weeks after Sashiko’s launch:

"As you say, Sashiko tends to be quite good. Even when it flags something unnecessarily and there's no actual problem, there's likely to be a reason for the question. And we've seen some truly stellar reports too. Things that are deep and subtle, and the AI is 100% correct. So anybody who thinks that all AI is slop is in denial about the current state." - Linus Torvalds (on lore.kernel.org)

What we learned from building and running Sashiko

First, benchmark-driven development beats intuition. While developing Sashiko, we tried many ideas that looked very reasonable on their face but didn’t end up working out. Other ideas were less obvious but worked surprisingly well. What was crucial: Early on, we built a benchmark out of nearly 1,000 real Linux kernel bugs and used it to evaluate every major Sashiko change. Every bug in this set was a real mistake that had passed human review by kernel experts, had been merged into mainline Linux, and later had to be fixed. On that benchmark, Sashiko with the new Gemini 4 Carbon model catches 75.8% of the bugs that human reviewers missed (using high thinking level).

Second, coding agents are not great at reviewing their own code. Models are trained to produce a working solution within a limited token budget. Asking these agents to review their own code might work well for isolated tasks, but for real, large codebases, creating a functional solution is often just 5-10% of the work. What’s really hard is to produce a solution that works all of the time, is well-integrated into the surrounding code, and doesn’t introduce subtle regressions. This is often substantially more complex and requires additional effort. Similar to human developers, agents benefit from external code review: Reviewers often spot issues that the initial author missed, even if they are not more experienced.

Third, open source and shared community ownership and development help to build trust. By being fully open and transparent from the beginning, Sashiko allowed anyone to run it the way they wanted: using different models (including open source and local models), customizing prompts, or even adopting Sashiko to other-than-Linux projects. This helped with community adoption and brought over 100 contributors to improve Sashiko, including some prominent kernel developers.

More and more engineers are putting local Sashiko instances into their coding-agent loops, so patches are checked against the community's review rules before a human maintainer ever sees them. We use the same workflow to build Sashiko itself ("Sashiko for Sashiko"), running it to review every change to its codebase and prompt pipeline both locally and through a Github integration.

Although Sashiko started in the Linux kernel, the need for an agentic trust layer applies across critical open-source software. Because the core review engine does not depend on C or on kernel-specific rules, the Linux kernel playbook (combining an open verification pipeline, community-owned domain guides, and a benchmark mined from historically known issues and fixes) can likely be applied to other foundational open-source projects such as GCC, LLVM, or Git.

"Now, I think the other side of AI - and this is where Sashiko comes in - is that it basically does end up being a tool that can then increase the trust in the patch. So AI giveth, and AI taketh away. But the basic issue shouldn't be AI per se, it should be that notion of 'trust'." - Linus Torvalds on LKML

You can check out Sashiko at sashiko.dev, or find the code on GitHub to run it in your own development workflow.

We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. items.content_excerpt: When looking to cut AI costs, teams often start with budgets or open-source models. But agent traces can reveal other opportunities to save. At Databricks, trace analysis surfaced several: offline replays showed no performance gain from upgrading from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, so we stayed on the cheaper 4.8; fixing common MCP errors recovered an estimated $1.2M in costs a year ; and traces showed that simple prompts were going to expensive models, prompting us to adopt Smart Routing . Today, we’re introducing Unity Gateway Insights , which automatically uses Genie to analyze millions of agent traces alongside your business data and ontology. It surfaces where tokens are being wasted: MCP errors that keep recurring, simple tasks running on expensive frontier models, and repeated workflows worth turning into shared skills, all in the context of your business and under the same governance as your other data. If you already have traffic flowing through Unity Gateway, open AI Gateway > Observability > Insights and generate a report for the last day, 7 days, or 30 days. Insights then writes a report on the tokenomics of your coding agent rollout that answers the following questions: You can add up to 10 questions of your own to a report, such as whether the newest model is worth it for your team's work. To dig further, continue the conversation with Genie. Ask which MCP server wasted the most tokens this month and who owns it, and you have a bug report ready to send. Finding this kind of waste requires a full record of every step of every agent session: inputs and outputs, tool calls, subagents, intermediate steps, latency, and token cost. A standalone gateway records only the requests that pass through it. Capturing the rest of each session means instrumenting every coding agent yourself, then exporting the traces to a data platform to analyze them. Pointing Claude Code at those traces still leaves you to design the investigation yourself, with no map of your business like the Genie Ontology provides. Insights runs the investigation we developed while rolling out coding agents to thousands of Databricks engineers. It samples sessions and groups them into workstreams by kind of work. Then it checks each workstream for failing MCP tools, bloated context, frontier models on simple tasks, and repeated workflows, and ranks what it finds by the tokens at stake. items.content_excerpt: Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how MonoKernels written in FlyDSL reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. A MonoKernel combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, mono means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by TileRT , the implementations discussed here use a persistent launch : a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. Both paths in Figure 2 can be replayed under HIP graphs. The difference is between multiple independent kernels and an author-designed persistent schedule within a launch. Some whole-kernel boundaries become finer-grained handoffs between portions of the computation. items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. items.content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. items.content_excerpt: Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at 13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed. Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for you). items.title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
items.summary: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.

items.title: Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build
items.summary: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.

items.title: Can Decision Models Replace LLMs in Real-World Contact Center Classification and Judging Tasks?
items.summary: Contact center systems often need to make bounded decisions, such as identifying a caller's intent, retrieving the knowledge-base article that answers a query, assessing agent compliance, or judging the output of AI models used in production. Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a promising cost-effective alternative to generative Large Language Models (LLMs) in such bounded conversational tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world contact center applications remains unclear. In this paper, we compare nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases: six classification tasks and two judging tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that many decision models can match the performance of frontier LLMs on contact center classification, and API-based closed decision models achieve this at the lowest per-request cost among the API models we evaluate. We further observe that their confident predictions are more accurate, enabling selective routing in real-world production scenarios. Across classification tasks, the main weakness of most decision models is abstention: they rarely choose the no-answer option, which accounts for most of their gap to the strongest LLMs (although Gemini-Decision-1 is the notable exception in this regard). We also find that the judging quality of decision models drops sharply for smaller models, and they are also more prone to position bias. In short, our findings provide practical guidance for selecting decision models based on abstention behavior, confidence, and deployment cost, rather than overall accuracy alone.

items.content_excerpt: You can’t run agents in production without governing the data they touch. When that data includes sensitive customer information, controlling access becomes a regulatory and contractual obligation. That puts engineering and security requirements at odds. Engineers need production traces to debug issues and improve agent performance. Security and compliance teams need to enforce least privilege: people should only see the data their job requires. That’s why we’ve added three new controls to LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data: Traces give engineers visibility into how an agent behaved and help them identify what needs to improve. When they record production activity, their inputs and outputs often contain sensitive customer data, such as names, health information, or payment details. Companies need to restrict access to this data to meet: First, they can create custom observability setups with duplicate traces and multiple workspaces. Engineers get trace access, but platform teams have more to configure and maintain. The alternative is to avoid sending traces to observability platforms altogether, preventing agent engineers from having visibility and slowing product velocity. We built these new controls so organizations can meet the needs of their engineering and security teams without the messy workarounds. Here’s how it works. You send your traces to LangSmith with full data fidelity, then grant access to only those who need it. items.content_excerpt: Think about how you work with a new hire. In their first week, you give them small, well-scoped tasks, like triaging a bug report or updating a doc. Soon you're giving them bigger tasks, and eventually you're handing them a lofty goal and letting them figure out how to tackle it. They still come to you with clarifying questions or review requests, just less often over time. Agents have gotten good enough that you can onboard them the same way, and like a good new hire, they're turning into proactive problem solvers. Personal agents like Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI's dots popularized proactive agents, which run in the background and work toward larger goals instead of waiting for a prompt. Hone puts it most directly, describing its Engines as AI that is "assigned goals rather than tasks." Goals let these agents take on harder problems that play out over days or weeks. A proactive agent still checks in with you when it's unsure what you want or needs your sign-off before something goes out. When your direct reports get really good at their jobs, you might find that you've become the bottleneck, and the same is true for agents. As they take on more goals, your attention becomes the scarce resource. We think two things are essential to building proactive agents that use it well: memory and UX. A few examples: Robin's reviews start from a real-world event, a newly opened pull request, and GTM Agent's daily brief runs on a schedule it created itself after a user requests one. We built both agents on Managed Deep Agents , where more than 70% of runs now come from schedules rather than an ad hoc human prompt. A proactive agent decides for itself when to come to you, and each check-in costs you some attention. It has to be proactive without being annoying . For an executive assistant agent that watches your inbox, that means flagging the message from your boss about tomorrow's launch without also flagging every newsletter. The agent can only tell the two apart if it knows what matters to you, and that knowledge comes from memory . Memory is the information an agent learns over time. items.title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.325
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Fixed a security issue in how zstd-compressed responses are decoded
  • Added a spinner tip in VS Code and similar integrated terminals about re-running a notebook cell, shown once Claude has read or edited a Jupyter notebook
  • Added a line under the error shown when your organization's policy blocks a request, saying how to continue: run /rewind and change the message, or run /clear
  • Added a note for Claude when a sandboxed git checkout, git stash or autostash pull cannot update protected files such as those in .claude
  • Fixed /security-review and skills' inline git commands stopping with an error in worktrees of bare repositories, --separate-git-dir checkouts and Android repo checkouts
  • Fixed subagents with their own model being moved to the plan-mode model when the model setting is opusplan or haiku
  • Fixed subagents on a different model sizing file reads and MCP results with the main session's model
  • Fixed sessions on many third-party gateways and Foundry stopping with a context length error on every turn instead of compacting
  • Fixed recent turns sometimes going missing from a resumed session after Claude Code stopped without a clean exit
  • Fixed shell commands running in the launch directory after the working directory was deleted; the command now fails with a message and can be re-issued
  • Fixed an approved plan edit being lost when the plansDirectory folder can't take it: the plan is now saved in the default plans folder, and a warning says where and why
  • Fixed a saved sonnet[1m] model setting being rewritten on a new install to a model id the API rejects
  • Fixed focus view hiding the reply to your prompt when a scheduled task replied after it
  • Fixed the prompt sometimes missing from a background subagent's view when fullscreen is off
  • Fixed long options in lists and permission prompts being partly overwritten when they wrap, and first-run screens losing lines on narrow terminals
  • Fixed startup warnings about permission rules and the "N MCP servers need authentication" notice being recorded as seen when they were scrolled out of view
  • Fixed the welcome header showing control characters or splitting across lines when an agent's name or the working folder contains them or a line break
  • Fixed the red error shown when Claude tries a command only you can run: a dim line now says it runs only when you type it at the prompt
  • Fixed /stats showing an Active days total that was one day too high
  • Fixed /insights saying a report was ready when no session qualified for analysis, and writing two values into its HTML report without escaping them
  • Fixed /voice saying voice mode changed when managed settings, --settings, or the project's .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json kept it as it was; it now says what holds it
  • Fixed the IDE welcome dialog showing Cmd+Esc for Quick Launch on Windows and Linux
  • Fixed Slack app tips showing when your organization's policy denies cloud sessions
  • Fixed claude purge hanging silently when there is no terminal to read keys from, and its project picker and -i prompts ignoring the keyboard when stdin is piped
  • Fixed claude plugin eval --output-dir '' writing the report into the current folder; it now exits with an error
  • Fixed claude -p text output on a terminal passing control sequences other than text styling; pipes and files are unchanged
  • Fixed leftover .oauth_refresh.lock.owner.tmp.* files piling up in the config directory
  • Fixed /fast saying "Fast mode has been disabled by your organization" under the keyless Console sign-in, where Claude Code had not asked the server
  • Fixed /model saying that your organization restricts a model when Claude Code could not check that, for example with no network
  • Fixed "Sign in with your Console account" in /login replacing your existing login when you pressed Esc right after the browser step
  • Fixed the browser showing the sign-in success page in some cases where sign-in failed or was canceled
  • Fixed claude auth status and other short commands leaving a lock behind on a Console profile, which made the next session hang for about a minute
  • Fixed background sessions started on your claude.ai login using (and billing) an API key or token from the shell that started the background service
  • Fixed more cases of a session moving to another sign-in in the background; these moves are now refused, with a message saying what works
  • Fixed a second Enter in the exit dialog stopping background work after the move to the background was refused
  • Fixed token counting on Amazon Bedrock sending the conversation to Bedrock when the allowedProviders managed setting does not allow it
  • Fixed AWS credential_process helpers and Google Cloud default credentials failing when Claude Code is started without a HOME environment variable
  • Fixed a session sometimes going back to an earlier permission mode after a subagent's plan was approved
  • Fixed one invalid value in an Agent SDK applyFlagSettings() call silently discarding all settings from earlier calls; a call that would do this is now refused with an error
  • Fixed sessions showing as waiting for input when a finished pull request only needed your own review or merge
  • Fixed an unrecognized teammateMode settings value being ignored without a warning: claude -p, the startup warning and claude doctor now list it as a skipped entry (still not applied)
  • Fixed --worktree skipping a WorktreeCreate hook from a plugin in CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR on the first run in a new home directory
  • Fixed brief-mode sessions, such as Dispatch, sending a reply again after the turn had already replied
  • Fixed Claude saying a working Atlassian, Asana or Sentry connector had failed in cloud sessions when a plugin listed it at a different URL
  • Fixed Claude Desktop and SDK sessions listing a folder's own MCP servers (.mcp.json, local) as host-added or not at all, and not connecting WebSocket ones, after a folder move or pre-warmed start
  • Fixed /mcp still listing a plugin's MCP server after a plugin reload removed it while it was connecting
  • Fixed an MCP server staying "needs authentication", and its mcp_tool hooks being skipped, after a token refresh that was refused only for a moment
  • Fixed MCP elicitation requests being cancelled without asking in headless mode after a server's connection was replaced during a tool call
  • Fixed MCP tool calls from an SDK host answering "Not connected" after a tool call had reconnected the MCP server
  • Fixed an MCP task getting stuck after its question was closed with Esc or asked again: the footer now says it needs your input, and Enter in /tasks shows the question again
  • Fixed background MCP tasks that stopped updating after another call to the same server lost the connection, when a later call reconnects
  • Fixed a background MCP task's question opening over a message you were still typing; it now waits until you send or clear the draft, and the spinner and turn timer keep running
  • Fixed worktree.sparsePaths and sparse plugin and marketplace clones leaving out the repository's root files on older git versions, such as 2.34
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions with several repositories being unable to use a repository added mid-session
  • Fixed Claude asking for permission before reading your own artifact or its data
  • Fixed deny and ask permission rules and hooks for the Artifact tool not applying in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts ignoring a worktree entered with EnterWorktree, writing ~ paths into the project, and leaving /mcp showing an MCP server as connected after its sign-in expired
  • Fixed words typed with a Yes at a permission dialog or plan approval not reaching Claude in Code Mode
  • Fixed Claude starting work by itself when you resumed a session that ended during a Code Mode script; it now waits for your next prompt
  • Fixed a missing OpenTelemetry user_prompt event for a message sent while tool calls run. The event has delivery.mode: "mid_turn" and the running turn's prompt.id
  • Fixed the OpenTelemetry user_prompt event leaving out earlier messages' text when queued messages merged into one turn in VS Code, or when one message had an image
  • Fixed a slash command's allowed-tools grants applying to background agents woken during or after its turn
  • Fixed /feedback and /bug to upload other sessions only when they were recorded by the signed-in account or organization
  • Fixed relative deny and ask permission rules (e.g. Read(./.env)) no longer covering the project after a cd; they now also apply in added directories
  • Fixed deny and ask permission rules starting with mcp__plugin_*_ missing a plugin's MCP server or tool spelled in another letter case
  • Fixed deny rules not being applied to a permission approval that arrives after Claude Code restarts, in self-hosted runner and claude remote-control sessions
  • Fixed a case where a committed .claude/settings.local.json could be treated as the user's own when Claude Code was started in certain subfolders of a repository
  • Fixed some deny and ask rules not applying to certain Bash commands
  • Fixed a gap in Bash permission checks where some compound commands could run without asking; these now ask for permission
  • Fixed a case where a Bash allow rule could run a different program than the one it names
  • Fixed a connector tool's approval prompt in cloud sessions being answered automatically while plugins were still loading
  • Fixed some subagents changing an artifact that people outside your organization can see, or uploading files to it, without asking first when an allow rule is set or uploads were approved earlier
  • Fixed some artifact publishes skipping the confirmation for pages that people outside your organization can see when "don't ask again" had been chosen for Artifact
  • Fixed auto mode judging only the first change to an artifact that people outside your organization can see; its yes now covers that change alone
  • Fixed a managed strictPluginOnlyCustomization lock on agents and skills not taking effect in sessions that were already running
  • Fixed sandboxed commands being able to write to the native updater's download folder in some cases
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a worktree's settings and hooks
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a linked worktree's shared git folder
  • Fixed /teleport's stash choice in some unusual git states: it now stops and says what to do
  • Windows: Fixed a start-up stall that could last about a second when a PATH entry sits under a folder your account cannot open
  • Fixed /resume on Windows refusing or hiding sessions whose folder was recorded with a different drive-letter case or slashes
  • Fixed an in-session /resume on Windows dropping a project's saved trust when the session was recorded with a different drive-letter case
  • Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when the working directory was below an allowRead folder inside a denyRead, such as under a symlinked home directory
  • Fixed Claude Desktop's third-party deployments staying on "Stopping" until a token renewal finished (once it includes this version)
  • Improved subagents cut off at the output token limit: they are now asked for the whole answer again, more briefly, instead of returning only its end
  • Improved startup with a keyless Console sign-in or other Anthropic profile login: a token that is still valid is read without waiting for the credentials lock
  • Improved the account email check: it now also refuses your email as a client's identity in scripts a command runs, file writes, web fetches and MCP calls
  • Improved the HTTPS authentication failed message for private plugin marketplaces: it now says git's terminal prompts and askpass programs are disabled, and it also appears with newer git versions
  • Improved the add-marketplace confirmations, plugin recommendation prompts and plugin install warning to say that plugins can run code on your computer, with access to your files and shell
  • Improved the claude --desktop sign-in error to name the API key, provider or setting that stops a Claude account sign-in from working
  • Improved the /voice "No audio detected" message on macOS and Windows: it now says where to pick your microphone
  • Improved MCP tasks: Claude is now told when a task is waiting for your answer, and can point you to /tasks
  • Improved claude remote-control: it now exits with status 4 when it stops by itself (single-session runs still exit 0) and 69 when it can't register, so a service manager can start it again
  • Improved the messages shown when a background session can't use its session's API key or token: they no longer suggest adding the key to settings
  • Improved the bundled dataviz skill's part-to-whole advice for static images and for parts with a natural order, such as age bands
  • Changed sandboxed Bash commands to follow the normal permission flow by default; set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true to keep running them without prompts
  • Changed managed settings that turn the sandbox on: to keep commands running without prompts, set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true in your highest-ranking managed source
  • Changed read-only git commands to ask first in a repository that isn't the project's or one you trusted; name it with --add-dir, not the additionalDirectories setting, to run them without prompts
  • Changed scheduled tasks and /loop to ask before running a skill that declares allowed-tools or hooks; add Skill(name) to permissions.allow to run it unattended
  • Changed "Always allow" in Desktop, IDE and SDK hosts: a rule alone is offered only when saving it would allow that command again, so a scheduled task that relied on one can now wait for you
  • Changed the sandbox to refuse sandboxed writes to .claude settings, skills, agents, commands and hooks in added directories, as it does in the launch folder
  • Changed worktree isolation: an isolated worktree session or agent is now refused git bisect run, git maintenance register|start and scalar's set-up commands, and is told what still works
  • Changed plugin MCP bundles (.mcpb, .dxt) to unpack under the plugins directory, not .mcpb-cache in the plugin's folder, so read-only plugin folders load; one fetched by URL downloads again once
  • Changed plugins of a remote marketplace that managed settings declare, enable and list in prependPlugins or appendPlugins to count as the organization's; pluginDigests is deprecated and ignored
  • Changed plugin loading to skip, and claude plugin validate to report, some unsafe paths and links in a plugin's folder
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders in --plugin-dir plugins no longer load from a session started above them; start Claude Code in the plugin folder instead
  • Changed EnterWorktree to refuse a WorktreeCreate hook path that goes through a symlink inside the project; have the hook print the real path
  • Changed tmux and iTerm2 teammates, and new sessions from the agents view opened with ←, to start in the session's folder instead of where the shell last ran cd
  • Changed prompt suggestions in the terminal to refresh less often after 8 turns in a row started by background or scheduled tasks, saving usage until you press a key or return to the terminal
  • Changed Esc on a background MCP task's question to "answer later": nothing is sent to the server, and the question stays in /tasks
  • Changed CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS to also set the context window of unrecognized model IDs that start with claude-, such as a gateway's claude-sonnet-latest
  • Changed /login to ask for permission to change your privacy settings
  • Changed /cost, $.session.usage(), --max-budget-usd and the cost and token metrics to count a mod's $.model.complete and $.model.classify calls
  • Changed the programs that Claude Code's sandbox starts for its own use, such as its network bridge, to run without Claude Code's sign-in tokens and API keys in their environment
  • Changed ripgrep, local git commands and the sandbox runtime's own helper programs to run without the mTLS client key's passphrase in their environment
  • Remote Control: Changed /resume and /teleport to disconnect first when the connected session has a share link, or when that can't be checked; run /remote-control to connect again
  • Changed Claude Code on the web, cloud scheduled tasks and Cowork cloud sessions to start despite sandbox.failIfUnavailable: the hosted container has no command sandbox
  • Changed requests for settings, permission rules, hooks or status over a cloud or self-hosted session's connection to return less or be refused; what applies in the session is unchanged
  • Changed claude -p with no cached account data to wait for that data before its first request, so a first run in a clean environment can start a few seconds later
  • Changed Claude's instructions to keep files you'll want out of its temporary scratchpad folder, which can be cleared
  • Changed marketplace ref to accept the full ID of any commit on a branch or tag; clients before this version can't clone such a pin, so a marketplace pinned this way stops loading there
  • Changed plugin marketplace and plugin downloads to use a CONNECT tunnel when ALL_PROXY is the only proxy set; a proxy that refuses CONNECT now fails them
  • Changed -p and SDK runs in a worktree or submodule mounted into a container to apply .claude/settings.local.json allow rules only once the folder is trusted
  • Changed self-hosted runners to refuse a session whose session folder or repository path is a symbolic link, other than a checkout hook's checkout
  • Removed "ask your admin to raise it" from spend limit and shared budget errors in cloud sessions and under Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Added prompt suggestions wherever the terminal shows them: Tab accepts the suggested next prompt; promptSuggestionEnabled: false in Claude Code's settings.json turns them off
  • [VSCode] Added a Console sign-in that creates no API key
  • [VSCode] Added a field to paste the redirect URL when signing in to an MCP server from the panel in SSH, WSL and container windows
  • [VSCode] Fixed the model picker's check mark staying on the old model after Claude Code restarted on another model or the model was switched over Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Fixed the effort selector offering levels above the effort cap set by your organization or the maxEffortLevel setting
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen offering sign-ins that the managed allowedProviders setting refuses
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt for MCP tools not saying why Claude Code asks when a safety check raises the question
  • [VSCode] Fixed the message for organization settings that couldn't load saying to run a command again; it now says to try again, matching the tab's Retry link
  • [VSCode] Improved the note shown for an untrusted folder: it now says why the extension is off and how to turn it on
  • [VSCode] Improved the error shown when the system refuses to run Claude Code: it now says your IT team can allow a blocked program
  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in card to say what to do when the browser shows a connection error for localhost
  • [VSCode] Changed the install link's marketplace confirmation button to "Trust marketplace and continue"
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed new cloud sessions cutting MCP tool descriptions loaded through tool search at 4,096 characters; the limit is now 16,384, as in other Claude Code sessions
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed artifact links pasted in Slack getting no card when the poster's Claude sign-in had expired in a workspace their organization doesn't manage; a plain card now appears
